extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, students of drama, and readers/students of literary theory interested in composing or evaluating tragedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama: how to construct plots, characters, diction, thought, spectacle and melody to produce pity and fear and accomplish catharsis. Focuses on formal rules (unity, magnitude), plot devices (peripety, discovery, suffering), and character construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy is 'the imitation of an action that is serious and also, as having magnitude, complete in itself; in language with pleasurable accessories... in a dramatic, not in a narrative form; with incidents arousing pity and fear, wherewith to accomplish its catharsis of such emotions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy must imitate a complete, serious action of sufficient magnitude, use language with rhythm/harmony/song where appropriate, be presented dramatically (not merely narrated), and include incidents specifically designed to arouse pity and fear so as to accomplish catharsis. Each element of this definition constrains choices of subject, form, and technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six formative parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The six parts of every tragedy are: 'a Fable or Plot, Characters, Diction, Thought, Spectacle and Melody.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the constitutive elements the poet must control. Two of them arise from the means (Melody and Diction), one from the manner (Spectacle), and three from the objects of imitation (Plot, Character, Thought). When evaluating a play, examine each part and how it contributes to the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important of the six is 'the combination of the incidents of the story' (the Plot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot is the 'life and soul' of tragedy: peripeties and discoveries (reversals and recognitions) are powerful attractions and central to tragic effect. Strong plot design can outweigh superior diction or character work; beginners often succeed first in diction/character but struggle with plot construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Plot (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole must have 'beginning, middle, and end.' A beginning is something not after anything else but with something after it; a middle is after something and has something after it; an end naturally follows something and has nothing after it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-constructed plot cannot begin or end arbitrarily: the sequence must form a natural whole. Each section should connect logically so the audience can apprehend the action as a single, coherent process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude / Suitable length
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is a matter of size and order; a story or Plot must be of a length 'to be taken in by the memory' and allow the hero to pass by a series of probable or necessary stages from misfortune to happiness, or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a span long enough to develop a complete action but short enough to be grasped as a unity. Excessively short or excessively vast plots lose the perception of unity and diminish tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action, not unity of subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The Unity of a Plot 'does not consist... in its having one man as its subject.' One must represent one action — a complete whole with closely connected incidents such that removing any one disjoins the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse a single protagonist with a single coherent action. Select and arrange episodes so they form one causally or probabilistically linked chain of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable or necessary incidents (poetic universals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's function is to describe 'a kind of thing that might happen, i.e. what is possible as being probable or necessary.' Poetry makes universal statements about what kinds of people will do in such circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot incidents should be credible as probable or necessary consequences of character and situation. The poet may adapt or invent names and circumstances but must maintain plausibility to convince the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodic plots are defective
rubrics_metrics.description: An episodic Plot is one 'when there is neither probability nor necessity in the sequence of episodes' and is regarded as the worst kind of simple plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stringing loosely connected episodes that lack causal or probable links. Episodes should be motivated and contribute to the central action; otherwise the work feels disjointed and inferior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Complex Plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are either simple or complex: 'simple' if the hero's change of fortune occurs without Peripety or Discovery; 'complex' if it involves Peripety, Discovery, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots (which include reversals and recognitions arising naturally from antecedents) are superior for tragic effect. Decide whether to aim for the more powerful complex structure or a restrained simple design and ensure devices arise from the plot itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripety (reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Peripety is 'the change from one state of things within the play to its opposite... in the probable or necessary sequence of events.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversals that logically follow from the plot's antecedents (e.g., Oedipus). A well-crafted peripety intensifies pity and fear and helps bring about the proper ending; avoid reversals that feel arbitrary or 'post hoc.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery (anagnorisis) and its species
rubrics_metrics.description: A Discovery is 'a change from ignorance to knowledge' (about persons or facts). The text lists species: (1) signs/marks, (2) poet-made/inartistic revelations, (3) memory-triggered recognition, (4) reasoning-driven discovery, (5) composite/bad-reasoning discoveries, and (6) the best kind—discoveries arising from the incidents themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer discoveries that arise organically from the incidents of the plot (most artistic). Avoid over-reliance on congenital marks or clumsy poet-driven expositional revelations; use memory or reasoning when they follow naturally from character and situation. Examples and rankings are given to illustrate relative artistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffering as a plot element
rubrics_metrics.description: Suffering is 'an action of a destructive or painful nature, such as murders on the stage, tortures, woundings, and the like.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suffering is one of the plot's parts (alongside peripety and discovery) and may be necessary to arouse pity and fear; determine whether such actions serve the plot's unity and moral logic rather than existing for spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid certain tragic-arc forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Three forms to be avoided: (1) a good man passing from happiness to misery; (2) a bad man passing from misery to happiness; (3) an extremely bad man falling from happiness into misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These forms fail to produce the required pity or fear: pity arises from undeserved misfortune and fear from the misfortune of one like ourselves. Choose a protagonist and arc that will plausibly evoke these emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal tragic protagonist (middle character and hamartia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The preferred hero is 'a man not pre-eminently virtuous and just' whose misfortune is 'brought upon him not by vice and depravity but by some error of judgement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a protagonist of high reputation but imperfect judgment so that his downfall feels both pitiable and possible (examples: Oedipus, Thyestes). The cause should be an error (hamartia) rather than moral depravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single issue and direction of change
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfect Plot 'must have a single... issue' and 'the change in the hero's fortunes must be... from happiness to misery' rather than a double story or opposite endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid double outcomes (parallel good/bad storylines with opposite resolutions). For a tragic effect, aim for a focused plot that drives toward a single catastrophic reversal from prosperity to ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter preference: familial horrors
rubrics_metrics.description: Deeds of horror carried out within the family (brother on brother, son on father, mother on son, etc.) are 'the situations the poet should seek after' because they most move pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing tragic material, favor conflicts and crimes among kin where betrayal, murder, or recognition produce stronger emotional responses than acts between enemies or strangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle's subordinate artistic role
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle is 'the least artistic of all the parts' and though an attraction, 'has least to do with the art of poetry.' The tragic effect is better produced by plot structure and incidents than spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not depend on spectacular stage effects to create pity/fear; aim to have the mere recital of incidents produce horror and pity. Spectacle may be used, but reliance on it for monstrous but unmotivated scenes indicates a weaker poet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters: four aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should (1) be good, (2) be appropriate, (3) be like the reality, and (4) be consistent and the same throughout (consistent inconsistency if that is the trait).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure what a person says or does reveals a moral purpose and that actions are probable or necessary consequences of character. Appropriateness means traits fit sex/role; likeness to reality means believable portrayal; consistency forbids arbitrary shifts unless explained by the character itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (intellectual content of speeches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is 'the power of saying whatever can be said, or what is appropriate to the occasion.' It is shown when characters prove a point or enunciate a general truth and is distinct from Character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate speeches for their appropriateness to the situation and their rhetorical effectiveness. Thought corresponds to the play's argumentative and thematic content and should serve action rather than replace it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (composition of verses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction means 'the composition of the verses' and is the expression of thoughts in words, practically the same in verse as in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language should suit the character and occasion; good diction enhances but cannot substitute for a properly constructed plot. Assess diction for clarity, appropriateness, and artistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody (musical elements) as pleasurable accessory
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody is 'the greatest of the pleasurable accessories of Tragedy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Musical elements (song, rhythm, harmony) augment tragic effect and should be integrated where appropriate, but they are accessory to the core dramatic imitation embodied in plot and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's craft: visualization, embodiment, and simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing plots and diction the poet should: (1) put the actual scenes as far as possible before his eyes; (2) act his story with gestures to feel the emotions; (3) simplify and reduce to a universal form before adding episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid visualization and physical embodiment to discover appropriate incidents and gestures; simplify to a universal core so episodes can be added appropriately; insert episodes only if they are appropriate and contribute to plot or character development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and brevity of episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes must be appropriate to the plot (e.g. the fit of madness leading to arrest) and, in plays, episodes are short; in epic poetry they serve to lengthen the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include episodes only when they support the plot's unity or elucidate character; keep subsidiary incidents brief in drama so they do not compromise coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denouement should arise from the plot (avoid artifice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Denouement (and the Denouement should arise out of the plot itself) 'and not depend on a stage-artifice'—artifice must be reserved for matters outside the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist deus ex machina or contrivances that resolve the action by means external to the story. Outcomes should be the necessary or probable consequences of prior incidents and character choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complication and Denouement (quantity/sectioning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy is in part Complication and in part Denouement: Complication = from the beginning to the point just before the change in the hero's fortunes; Denouement = from the beginning of the change to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When structuring a play, clearly identify the turning point separating complication and denouement to preserve pacing and ensure the change in fortune is earned and coherent.
